stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

 "path": "continual_arc_task_d567de38.md",
 "content": "# Continual-ARC task pattern: tiled junction lattice (task-d567de38)

Observed rule from three demos and confirmed test:

1. In the large input, identify the regular grid of junctions where the thick separator lines cross. The input is an enlarged encoding; each junction is a lattice node. Junctions may be at the ends/edges as well as internal crossings (e.g. test x=0,11,22 and y=0,7,14,21,28).
2. Form every sliding 2×2 block of adjacent lattice nodes. Each such block becomes one output cell, so output dimensions are (number of junction rows − 1) × (number of junction columns − 1).
3. If all four junction colors in that 2×2 block are the same, put that color in the output cell. Otherwise put the ordinary room/interior fill color (the dominant non-separator color, e.g. 9 in test/demo 1, 3 in demo 2, 2 in demo 3).

- Demo 1 output 6×3: every pair of adjacent row/column junction intervals becomes a pixel; uniform 2×2 marker blocks become 7, 4, or 3, mixed blocks become 9.

- Demo 3 output 1×1: its sole relevant 2×2 junction block is uniformly 0, so output [[0]].
- Solved test: junction lattice y=[0,7,14,21,28], x=[0,11,22], background=9. Applying the rule gives [[9,5],[5,9],[9,9],[9,4]] (verified correct).

Useful caution: include outer-edge junction nodes; the lattice is not just internal colored intersections. Do not read every junction directly as an output pixel—output pixels test uniformity over each 2×2 group."
